Ministerial Labour
min-i-STEER-ee-uhl LAY-ber
noun
From ministerial (of a minister) + labour; the diligent toil of the minister in the Word and in the care of the church.

📖 Biblical Definition

Ministerial labour is the diligent, often costly toil of the minister of Christ in the Word and in the care of the church—the work, not the mere title or office, of those who serve as elders and preachers. Paul presses the labour of the ministry: the elders that rule well are worthy of double honour, especially they who labour in the word and doctrine; he charges Timothy, Study to shew thyself approved unto God, a workman that needeth not to be ashamed, rightly dividing the word of truth; and he describes his own ministry as labour, striving according to His working, which worketh in me mightily. The work is no light thing: the diligent study and preparation of the Word, the toil of preaching and teaching, the watching over souls, the wrestling in prayer, the bearing of the care of all the churches, the enduring of hardship and reproach. It is called a good work—if a man desire the office of a bishop, he desireth a good work—but a laborious one, demanding the whole man. The labourer is worthy of his hire, and the church is to esteem and support those who spend themselves in this toil. The dictionary honors ministerial labour as the diligent, sacrificial work of the faithful minister—in study, preaching, prayer, and the care of souls—against the notion of the ministry as ease or mere position, and presses both the minister to labour and the church to honour and uphold those who labour in the word and doctrine.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

The diligent, costly toil of the minister in the Word and the care of the church; not title or ease but labour—study, preaching, prayer, the watching over souls.

📖 Key Scripture

1Ti 5:17 — "Let the elders that rule well be counted worthy of double honour, especially they who labour in the word and doctrine."

2Ti 2:15 — "Study to shew thyself approved unto God, a workman that needeth not to be ashamed, rightly dividing the word of truth."

Col 1:29 — "Whereunto I also labour, striving according to his working, which worketh in me mightily."

1Co 15:10 — "But by the grace of God I am what I am: and his grace which was bestowed upon me was not in vain; but I laboured more abundantly than they all: yet not I, but the grace of God which was with me."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

The ministry is treated as ease, title, or status; Scripture makes it diligent labour in the Word and the care of souls, demanding the whole man.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The corruption is the notion of the ministry as ease, title, or status—a position of honour without the toil, a platform without the study, a name without the work. But Scripture everywhere speaks of the ministry as labour. Paul does not commend the elders who merely hold office but they who labour in the word and doctrine (1 Tim 5:17), and he describes his own ministry as striving and toiling: I laboured more abundantly than they all (1 Cor 15:10).

The principle to recover is the diligent, sacrificial character of true ministerial work. The minister is a workman, charged to study to shew himself approved unto God, rightly dividing the word of truth (2 Tim 2:15)—and study, here, is no idle word but earnest toil. The work demands the whole man: the labour of preparing and preaching the Word, the wrestling in prayer, the watching over souls, the bearing of the care of the churches, the enduring of hardship. Paul labours, striving according to God’s working in him (Col 1:29). It is a good work, but a costly one. Therefore the church is to esteem and uphold those who spend themselves in it, counting them worthy of double honour, and the minister is to give himself wholly to the labour—not to the ease of office but to the toil of the Word.
